mcqs.question: Why can't a mobile client's networking layer just copy a backend-to-backend service's assumptions?
options: A mobile client should assume the link is unreliable, variable, and has a battery cost per request, unlike a stable always-on backend link
Mobile devices use a different version of the HTTP protocol than backends
Backend services never need retry logic, so mobile doesn't need it either
Mobile networking is strictly a subset of backend networking with no additional concerns
mcqs.explanation: A mobile client faces an unreliable, variable-bandwidth link where every request also has a radio energy cost beyond its bytes — assumptions a backend-to-backend call, on a stable data-center link, never has to make. Both use the same HTTP/TCP fundamentals; the difference is the environment around them.

mcqs.question: Why do ten isolated 1KB requests cost more battery than one 10KB request, even though the total bytes transferred are the same?
options: Smaller requests are always compressed less efficiently
TCP handshakes are ten times slower for small payloads
Each isolated request either pays a fresh radio ramp-up cost or extends an expensive high-power tail period, and that ramp/tail cost dominates for small, spread-out requests
The device's CPU has to parse ten separate response headers
mcqs.explanation: The radio's ramp-up and tail-time costs are roughly fixed per active period regardless of payload size, so spreading the same bytes across many isolated requests multiplies that fixed cost, while one batched request pays it once. It's a radio-power effect, not a protocol-parsing one.

mcqs.question: A list screen needs each item's nested detail fields, and the fields needed vary by screen. Which API style most directly avoids client-side N+1 calls here?
options: REST with one endpoint per resource type
gRPC, because binary framing eliminates the need for multiple requests
GraphQL, because the client can request exactly the nested fields it needs across the whole list in a single query
REST with pagination
mcqs.explanation: GraphQL lets the client specify exactly which nested fields it needs in one round trip, which is precisely the batching problem a REST client would otherwise solve with one call per item. gRPC's binary framing helps latency and throughput but doesn't by itself solve varying, nested field selection the way GraphQL's query shape does.

mcqs.question: Why is exponential backoff with jitter preferred over an immediate, fixed-interval retry after a mobile request fails?
options: Fixed intervals are technically impossible to implement on mobile radios
Jitter is required by app store review guidelines
An immediate or synchronized fixed retry wastes radio wakeups into a still-degraded connection and can cause many clients to retry in lockstep, overwhelming a server that just recovered
Backoff eliminates the need for idempotency keys entirely
mcqs.explanation: Backoff with jitter spaces out retries so they don't hammer a still-troubled connection or synchronize across many clients into a retry storm against a recovering server. It addresses timing and load, not correctness of repeated non-idempotent operations, which idempotency keys handle separately.

mcqs.question: A team pins their app to a single leaf certificate with no backup pin, then rotates that certificate during a routine renewal. What happens?
options: Every installed copy of the app rejects the backend's new certificate and loses connectivity until an app update ships with the new pin
The app automatically falls back to standard CA-based trust
Nothing changes, since certificate pinning only applies to debug builds
The backend silently continues accepting the old certificate to stay compatible
mcqs.explanation: Pinning rejects anything except the pinned certificate or key, so rotating without a pre-shipped backup pin locks out every installed app instance simultaneously until a new release ships — this is exactly why teams pin the CA's public key and always ship a backup pin ahead of rotation.

mcqs.question: A checkout POST request times out from the client's perspective, but the server actually processed it before the response was lost. What prevents a naive retry from creating a duplicate order?
options: An idempotency key generated client-side and sent on every retry of that logical operation, so the server recognizes the duplicate and returns the original result
Switching the endpoint from POST to GET
Increasing the client-side timeout so this never happens
Exponential backoff alone, by spacing retries far enough apart
mcqs.explanation: An idempotency key lets the server tell "this is the same logical operation retried" from "this is a genuinely new order," regardless of how the network behaved in between — which backoff timing alone cannot do, since the underlying request is still non-idempotent without it.
